title: API rate limiter
summary: Distributed counters with token buckets at the gateway.
prompt: Design a rate limiter for a public API: each API key gets a quota (for example 100 requests per second and 1M per day). Over-limit requests are rejected quickly and clearly.

requirements: Functional: enforce per-key limits over several windows, return 429 with Retry-After, and let operators change limits without deploys.
Non-functional: add under a few milliseconds per request; work across many gateway instances; degrade safely if the limiter store fails.
estimation: 1M requests/s across 100 gateways; each request needs one counter operation.
10M API keys × a few counters × ~100 bytes ≈ a few GB in a shared in-memory store.
api: Response headers: RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, and Retry-After on 429.
Admin: PUT /limits/{plan} to change a plan’s quotas.
data: Token bucket per key: (tokens, last_refill) in a shared in-memory store, with a TTL so idle keys disappear.
Limit configuration per plan, cached on gateways and refreshed every few seconds.
design: The gateway authenticates the key, looks up its plan, and calls check() before forwarding.
check() runs an atomic script in the store: refill tokens by elapsed time × rate, then take one if available.
The store is sharded by API key, so each key’s state lives on one shard.
deepDives: Algorithms: a fixed window is cheap but lets twice the limit through at window edges; a sliding-window counter weights the previous window to approximate a true sliding window; a token bucket allows controlled bursts.
Atomicity: separate read and write calls race across gateways; do the read-modify-write in one atomic operation or script.
Latency: for very high rates, gateways can take small token batches locally and sync periodically, trading exactness for speed.
bottlenecks: One very hot key overloads one shard: use local pre-allocation for that key.
Store outage: fail open for most traffic (availability) but fail closed for sensitive endpoints such as login.
Clock differences: use the store’s time, not each gateway’s.
tradeoffs: Exact global counting costs a network hop per request; local approximations are faster but can overshoot briefly.
Fail open risks overload; fail closed risks an outage caused by the limiter itself.
Token buckets are friendly to bursty clients; fixed windows are easier to explain to customers.

rubric.text: Chose an algorithm and explained its burst behaviour.
Kept counters in a shared store and made updates atomic.
Returned 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers.
Kept added latency within a stated budget.
Decided fail-open vs fail-closed per endpoint.
Handled hot keys and local token pre-allocation.
